A supernatural horror story where you use a missing person's phone (texting contacts/viewing photos/reading e-mail/other apps or social media) to figure out what happened to them. Not the same but it gives a similar feel to me as a game like Orwell.

I don't really enjoy horror games in general so I preferred playing this game as a mystery. I didn't really care for the random 'horror' sound effects or imagery. I was a bit disappointed when the plot went for [spoiler]the sci-fi twist. It's alright but I would have liked a regular, more realistic thing. It felt like something outside of your control with no real foreshadowing or buildup. There is nothing to suggest that it was possible and even after you learn about it you can't go back and see much in a new light. It might be nice if they at least put something random about the dangers of AI or something.[/spoiler]

Aside from the general phone-searching there are some minigames. They aren't too tough but one might be harder if you're not a native english speaker. One minigame is taking a jumbled list of words and making the right sentence out of it. However, it's not enough to get an equivalent meaning- you have to get the word order exactly right. For example, 'Meet me and I'll show ya this weekend' is wrong but 'Meet me this weekend and I'll show ya' is right.

Worth a look if you're fine with learning about the missing person story through phone history and dialogue.

Other thoughts:[list]
[*] It's a little annoying that in order to get the 'good' ending you have to [spoiler]manipulate people because there's no way to convince them otherwise.[/spoiler]
[*] I would have liked multiple save slots.
[*] It's nice that it can be set to automatically skip text on repeat playthroughs.
[*] Pretty much no settings to adjust (only subtitles). I would've liked at least volume and resolution options.
[*] Some inconsistencies/strange things: [spoiler]She met Taylor on Spark but had been following him on Jabbr 3 months ago. Cassie's AMA from 3 months ago is still continuing even though it closed (you get to ask a question)? The article mentions a back-and-forth between genders but you're forced to repeat the female gender and use one of the three pre-selected photos (it seems like other pictures don't progress the story). Why is it assimilating the 'weak'? From what I understand it's somehow taking control of a person and building a world out of their simulacrum (online personification?)? And then discarding the physical body for some reason because they can only lure in one person on Spark before they're useless?[/spoiler]
[*] A bunch of grammar and spelling errors and incorrect subtitles.
[*] Only crashed randomly once.
[/list]

My first experience with the found phone game genre was disappointing. I found [I]Replica[/I] to be an undercooked, preachy, borderline sciolistic game that is best not played. My excitement for this genre was quashed quickly, but I remembered that I still have [I]SIMULACRA[/I] in my backlog of games. Because of that, I decided to give found phone games another try.

Coincidentally, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] was partly inspired by [I]Replica[/I] (as seen by the titles), and partly by [I]Her Story[/I], one of my favourite games of all time. I loved [I]Her Story[/I] for its intriguing narrative and presentation, so I had some hope for [I]SIMULACRA[/I]. Thankfully, after my disheartening first exposure to found phone games, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] did not disappoint.

[I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a mystery game, in which you find a phone that belongs to a woman named Anna. By digging deep into her personal life chronicled by the contents of her phone and Internet activities, you uncover clues as to why Anna had gone missing. The puzzles in this game are fun, fair, and hardly difficult. Because of that, the game manages to present the story in a nice flow. It also helps that [I]SIMULACRA[/I] has a slick presentation, with a clean, Android-like user interface that controls well with mouse and keyboard. The in-game videos are pretty well done, too, but I did find the voice acting for one particular character to be laughable.

Despite [I]SIMULACRA[/I] being described or classified as a horror game, I did not find it scary.  Aside from a few instances, in which some players may find the game's version of a "jump scare" frightening, I considered this game to be more suspenseful. You can feel the plot thickening and tension building as the game progresses, with some subtle (but usually not so subtle) graphical and audio alterations making the game increasingly unnerving. The way [I]SIMULACRA[/I]'s story unfolds is almost Hitchcockian.

As much as I enjoyed the game narrative, I did find the ending slightly abrupt. It seemed like there is more story to tell, and perhaps the spin-off game, [I]SIMULACRA: Pipe Dreams[/I], may tie up some loose ends. Still, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a very enjoyable game, made even better if played in the dark with earphones on. The developers smartly included a "Begin+" mode that will unlock after the first playthrough. This mode allows you to replay the entire game with sped-up text, so you can retry certain scenarios without needing to sit through the slow, deliberate pace of the chat sessions. (It's also a time saver for achievement hunters.) [I]SIMULACRA[/I] gets an enthusiastic recommendation from me.

P.S.: I wrote this review after completing [I]Sara is Missing[/i] the predecessor of this game. [I]SIMULACRA[/I] shares many similarities with [I]S.I.M.[/I] (Coincidence? I think not!), and [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is clearly more refined in both story and game mechanics. Both games are worth playing, as they are both good ambassadors for the found phone game genre.

A very interesting and well done horror game about fiddling with a stranger's phone.

Before Simulacra, the devs made Sara is Missing, a game following the same line (horror game about exploring someone's phone) and, in Simulacra, it's easy to notice how much the game has evolved. While in SIM there were some choices to be made but ultimately they didn't change all that much, in the case of Simulacra it actually changes, with 4 possible different endings depending on what you do during the game.

The game involves talking to people using the phone's messenger app, browsing through other apps, searching for clues and solving some puzzles, while experiencing some creepy things on the way. The story, although somewhat linear (with some differences based on your choices) is interesting and well done. Beating the game once also allows the player to start a new game with faster text speed, which allows for faster playing in order to obtain the different endings.

I think the only two things I feel the game could have done better is that, first, it could have been a little more creepy. Not that it's not creepy - it certainly is - but it's also a little predictable. It could have had some less predictable moments like [spoiler]weird messages showing up in the middle of normal conversations, creepy pictures/videos opening out of nowhere, etc[/spoiler]. The second thing being that there are a few conversations (not many however - just a few) that go on for longer than they need to, sidetracking into subjects that aren't ultimately important when you're trying to find a missing person.

Nonetheless, a very good game and easily worth its asking price.

Also, for anyone who likes this game, I'd also suggest the free game they have released also from the Simulacra series, called "Simulacra: Pipe Dreams".

I'm a big fan of found-phone games, and had previously enjoyed Sara Is Missing. SIMULACRA is an extension of those horror-tendrils into the tiny genre, and definitely ranks well amidst other contenders like Unrd (Last Seen Online, The Silent Truth, My Last Three Days, Now Live, etc etc), Replica, the Normal Lost Phone series, and so forth. (It should be noted that I also count alternate OS and hacking games in this genre when it allows for entrance into a character's private computer; Mainlining and Orwell definitely contribute to the genre in substantial ways--)

This one has a great narrative pushing it forward, but the big stumbling block comes from the clunky puzzle integration. Content in the phone is corrupted, and appears as fragmented photographs and jumbled up text messages that need your help in piecing back together. These broke the immersion of the game in ways that Normal Lost Phone, Unrd, and Orwell all avoided. Password puzzles were more believable, but I felt that if the developers had added something like 'download a decrypting software' or something like this, and then integrated the gamification/puzzles into that as a feature/way to pass the time, I would've received that far better than the literal piecing-together. Another issue with that was how it forcibly slowed down playthroughs on repeat-plays for the different endings. Despite these extremely minor flaws, the great acting and overall game design definitely proved to be an engaging time-eater. Websites looked and behaved believably, characters were hilarious and genuine, you found yourself caring for Anna amidst all these weirdos. I hope to see the primary antagonist's motivations and development played out over future games, as I don't believe this is the end of their story. Definite thumbs up from me.

As the game progresses, your paranoia is fed more unnerving facts. This guy acts weird, right? Do you really trust him? Isn't he actually psycho rapist? And what about the other guy? What are his plans?

If it would stop there, it would be so good, but the story is unfortunately ruined by terrible, unsatisfying conclusion, and all that build-up atmosphere just vanishes and you stare at the screen like "are you kidding me Mr. Developer couldn't you think of something even cheesier" and you can't help but think about your high school essays where you couldn't think of proper ending of a story so you just shoved some aliens in there and hoped nobody would care.

Anyway the premise and execution are still quite good and I am fully aware that my opinion of the story can be just my personal preference.

Lately, I've gone down a weird rabbit hole of buying/playing cheap games on Steam. That aside, the game was pretty fun. The acting was a bit cheesy and there were some pretty obvious grammatical errors, but I mean, it's an indie game. All things considered, it was enjoyable and well worth the $2. I don't know why, exactly, but I enjoy these little games where you have to explore someone's life through their cell phone. I'll definitely check out the other games from this developer.

I don't know how I missed this one when it first came out. I've played a couple of these titles that have you navigating a lost phone (A Normal Lost Phone, Another Lost Phone: Laura's Story, Replica, etc.), and generally find the premise captivating, even if I have some irritations with the details of each game. In addition, SIMULACRA was quite well received on Steam. At the time of this writing, the game has 96% positive reviews overall!

As I began to explore, there was a lot to like about the game. The phone felt "real," and I thought that the Apps that were present were a good reflection of what many young people have installed. I enjoyed the "de-scramble" puzzles that allow you to decrypt texts and photos, although a few of the text puzzles seemed like they should have multiple solutions. Lastly, I thought that the sound design was brilliant. Periodic background sound effects keep the player tense and worried about their exact location while perusing the phone's contents. Lastly, the sound effect recorded by Greg in Anna's home (also used later in the game) is just so unnerving. The game does an excellent job of creating an unsettling tone.

But of course, there were a number of things I didn't like as well. I felt that the game could be a bit too linear during the majority of the playthrough - you often were forced to have dialogue with either Greg or Taylor before the game would progress, even if you weren't particularly interested in talking with them. I thought it felt strange to receive calls on the phone and be unable to answer. Afterwards, the caller would typically ask you by text why you didn't answer, and you typically would respond with something like, "I couldn't understand what you were saying." However, I never felt that I had difficulty understanding what was said - the game just didn't provide me with the means to respond. Lastly, I just wasn't particularly impressed with the videos of Anna. Perhaps the actress was asked to adhere too closely to a script, but her video blogs did not feel very organic to me.

Luckily, I found the final act of SIMULACRA to be absolutely fascinating. I want to refrain from spoiling the game for anyone, but the game has something important to say about conformity and romantic desirability in the digital age. Real life has a "messiness" that can easily be omitted in our curated digital worlds. Do we lose our humanity through this omission? What if we did?

Simulacra is another game within the sara is missing universe. The first game was good but with new additions to a series brings new mechanics and fixes the short commings of the original, does this game do just that? I will be reviewing the game with a pro/ con style and end with my conclusion.

Pro:
     The game is very creepy. Now jumpscares are cheap and something I dont really enjoy but the game has ambient sound effects that are very spooky. Sometimes you may hear nocking at a door or a wisper or see the lights flicker in your field of view. Some are not really strong in spooking the player but the sound effects really sell the horror.

      The plot is good. Now this is pretty much a horror thriller game that delves with a deep mystery. The game throws you for many loops making you question who can you trust and how much information you should provide. You never know who is at the other end of that text message you recieved. The further you go the deeper the rabbit hole goes.

        The gameplay is simplistic. A game having a simplistic gameplay is nothing to fear. This is like playing a tale tell game where you get dialogue options but sometimes it effects the response of other players and the ending. There are branching paths but not many to get more than 2ish playthroughs. Still it is good to see that some choices creates a response that effect the story and feels a bit like a genuine response in a hypothetical world.

Con:
      There are some puzzles that are difficult. This game has quite a few moments that test memory and makes you search for clues to progress but some of these clues are very well hidden meaning in order to progress you might need to search the internet for the solution to save the frustration. It is a minor issue but i swear there is this one puzzle i could never solve.

Conclusion:
       In short this game is short but it is a blast to play. The story is creepy with atmoshere and has a great story. If you play the game for just a short ammount of time you will be hooked into finding out the truth. I can not reccomend this game enough for anything curious in the game. It is resonably priced in retrospect to how long the game is.

SIMULACRA doesn't disappoint! I don't like to watch "Let's Play's" or anything before playing games because they tend to ruin some of the fun and that certainly is the case here. A lot of the complains I read from players is that they knew what was coming ahead of time... I had no idea and some of the things happening in my headphones genuinely terrified me because I legitimately thought they were happening in my house. I won't spoil what they were for anyone who has yet to play.

Still, like Sara is Missing, I think more can be done with this genre. The apps are fun to play with for a few minutes but it becomes apparent pretty quickly how shallow and underdeveloped they are. The dialogue is quite obviously written by someone to whom English is a second language and they didn't have anyone who speaks English proofread it. Lots of obvious typos and grammatical errors kind of took me out of the atmosphere. The voice acting by one of the characters is over the top to the point that it's cringey. The main character, though, is wonderfully acted and I couldn't tell at first that she wasn't actually American.

Although this hasn't dethroned The Black Watchmen for the title of my favorite alternate reality game, SIMULACRA is worth a play for anyone who's looking for something spooky, casual, immersive, and a bit of a brainteaser. The price point can't be beat, though I will say that I suspect that playing the appstore version on your phone would probably be more immersive than playing it over Steam.

The story starts with you finding a phone belonging to an attractive girl named Anna. You're allowed to navigate through her email account, her texts, her pics/vids, and various social media accounts, and you quickly figure out that something is seriously amiss. As you contact her friends, ex-boyfriend and other acquaintances you understand that your role as the player is to do quite a lot of snooping and social engineering to uncover whatever happened to Anna. Your choices are saved throughtout the play and shape the ultimate outcome of the story - I believe there are 4 different endings.

You do need to play it a bit smart; at points you will need to obtain access to accounts and people that are not obvious, which may require you to dig deeper into photos and media feeds to discover the information you need. I did not find any of the 'puzzles' overly difficult, but a few did give me some pause while I dug up the information needed to continue.

There is both live acting and voice acting throughout the game, so you definitely need your sound on to play. Some of the voice acting seems very forced (and some voice actors in particular are rather annoying to listen to) but the pics and vids felt real enough and the chats you have with other characters did a good job of giving each one a solid personality.

There is a horror element to the story, but I did not see any overt gore or violence from my own playthrough. There is something of a jumpscare towards the end, but nothing too bad. Lots of Exorcist style demon-grumbling, static, spooky messages and so on to set the mood as you go.

So overall, for the price, it's a worthwhile buy if this type of game appeals to you.
